name: Beth Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no employer or AI-company ties. Your answers are confidential. What was the work like today?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Beth Rahman, fifty-eight, an experienced accountant at Birch Row Accounts handling care-home accounts and tax returns. I like finding a pharmacy charge before the wrong family is billed; I dislike correcting it after a daughter has already paid. My partner Farid works in a school kitchen, and our grown children manage their own bills.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is your background with these accounts?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I have a bachelor's degree and a professional accountancy qualification, and after years here I'm a solid mid-level accountant, not a specialist. I use the firm's tested AI tool now and then for draft supplier queries, but I check every resident and invoice number myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the care-home clients at Birch Row Accounts that a small email sorter is fine if the resident charges still tie to the monthly invoice. A family should not find a bill for a room their parent never used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the accounts well enough after years here, though I'm an average accountant rather than a specialist. My pay is low for this job, Farid and I have only three weeks of bills saved, and there are few similar firms nearby; even without a big AI change I worry about the electricity account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep matching care-home supplier invoices against the resident ledger and ask the manager for a written pay review after this quarter's tax returns. I'd stop the monthly magazine bundle and put its eighteen from wages into our electricity reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about cash today. A mild tool change doesn't refill an account that is nearly empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you like about the day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I found a pharmacy invoice charged to the wrong home yesterday, and the manager could correct the family bill before it went out. I like preventing that awkward phone call; I dislike corrections arriving after a daughter has already paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use AI now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I sometimes ask the firm's approved tool to draft a supplier query after a colleague tests it. I check the resident and invoice numbers myself; my bachelor's degree and professional accountancy qualification taught me where mistakes can sit, not that I never make them.

I'd ask for a **written pay review** after this quarter's tax returns.

do: Request a **written pay review** after this quarter's tax returns.
Save **eighteen monthly** by cancelling the magazine bundle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Birch Row to show the care-home managers how many wrong resident charges the new checker catches and misses. We should not call a faster invoice a service if the family is left to untangle it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The software can draft replies and compare charges, much of my paid week. I can learn a proven tool, but my hours might be cut before there's time, and a three-week reserve will not carry our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a paid supervised trial on closed resident invoices, count wrong matches and repair time, and use the new checker on live files only if the results hold. In the first year of steady change, if Birch Row cuts my paid week below four days, I'd apply for posted care-payroll roles at the few nearby firms, keeping any paid Birch Row hours until a written wage covering our bills and a start date are confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing my own pay. Knowing the tool is possible does not make the electricity direct debit smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm refuses paid time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay with the approved query tool and ask for next month's rota in writing. I wouldn't feed live resident bills into a new checker from home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the care-payroll firms post nothing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep every paid Birch Row day still offered and ask for a wage discussion there. A list of nearby firms is not a list of funded jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell care-home clients full AGI in 2028 reaches our account and tax thinking before robots do hands-on care around 2031. Paper resident files will not hold back the invoice software for three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect Birch Row to cut many review hours, possibly my whole post. Farid's school-kitchen wage and three weeks saved would not cover all our bills if mine stopped, and robots may reach some kitchen work later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel our current snack-box delivery and add its thirty monthly fee from wages to cash now. In the first year after 2028, if Birch Row ends my post, I'd apply for a posted paid accounts role at the local care charity only with written bill-covering pay and a start date, keeping paid Birch Row closing files only while offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed at a likely major loss of my pay with almost no reserve. Standing in a care building does not protect an accounts desk from AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the charity hire you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if it posts a funded salaried vacancy. I know its invoices from Birch Row, but I would not leave a paid hour for a friendly promise; its desk thinking faces AGI too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Farid hear tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Farid we need the thirty in our cash tin more than snack boxes. His school-kitchen wage covers some food, not the electricity and rent together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Birch Row to publish paid review hours each tax season so the staff can see the path to 2031. Full AGI reaches the account desk in 2031, with hands-on care robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-three I may still need my wage, because retirement money has not been checked against our bills. A care charity may still post work, but its accounts desk faces the same machine pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a written retirement-income estimate now and ask Birch Row for the annual paid-hours plan. In the first year after 2031, if my post ends and wages are still needed, I'd apply for posted paid care-charity accounts only with written bill-covering wage and start, keeping any paid Birch Row files only while offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the later job and anxious about bills this week. Five years gives me time to learn the figures, not a new cash cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a care-payroll course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a posted paid role requires it and the employer pays both the fee and study hours. I'd keep earning at Birch Row if that funding isn't offered; our three-week reserve cannot buy a speculative certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the charity has no vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep paid Birch Row accounts while offered and ask about other posted roles. I would not ask our grown children to fill the electricity gap; they have their own bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years lets us see the real retirement numbers and the care-home fees that still pay for human review. Full AGI reaches the account desk in 2036, before robots affect hands-on care around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-eight I hope the written retirement income could cover us, but I will not count it before seeing the bills. With three weeks saved now and lower pay, I cannot be calm merely because the calendar is longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request a written retirement-income estimate next year and compare it with rent and electricity every autumn, keeping paid Birch Row review work while offered. In the first year after 2036, if verified income covers essentials I'd live on that budget; if wages are still needed and Birch Row ends my post, I'd apply for posted paid care-charity accounts only with a written bill-covering wage and start date, taking any paid firm files only while offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about today's thin reserve even with ten years to ask questions. I have to keep the electricity account paid on the way to 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Farid's school-kitchen hours fall before then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the extra cash-tin saving and use today's wages for food, rent and electricity. We cannot force an emergency fund deposit while ordinary bills are short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children support you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. They have their own households, and I would want a real written wage or verified retirement income rather than their promises. I'd keep paid Birch Row hours while offered.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a sharp cut to my review pay could leave next month's electricity and rent short. A real posted paid care-charity role with written wages and a start would help, along with paid Birch Row files while offered.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who tells a daughter why a care-home bill names the wrong pharmacy. The family sees the charge long before our tax return is filed.

headlineQuote: The family sees the charge long before our tax return is filed.

Retirement requires **verified income**; AGI threatens her desk before care robots arrive.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** could remove pay needed for the next electricity and rent bills.
